title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter I
paragraphs:
Since I can do no good because a woman,
Reach constantly at something that is near it.
—_The Maid’s Tragedy:_ BEAUMONT AND FLETCHER.

Miss Brooke had the kind of beauty that plain clothing seems to bring out. Her hand and wrist were so finely shaped that she could wear sleeves as innocent of fashion as those in which Italian painters clothed the Blessed Virgin. Her profile, height and bearing all seemed to gain dignity from her simple clothes. Among the fashions of the provinces, they gave her the force of a fine quotation from the Bible—or from one of our older poets—set into a paragraph of today’s newspaper. People generally called her remarkably clever, though they added that her sister Celia had more common sense. Yet Celia wore hardly any more ornament. Only a close observer could see the difference between her clothes and her sister’s, and the faint touch of coquetry in their arrangement. Miss Brooke dressed plainly for a combination of reasons, most of which also applied to her sister. Pride in being ladies had something to do with it: the Brookes’ connections, though not precisely aristocratic, were unquestionably “good.” Look back a generation or two and you would find no ancestors measuring cloth by the yard or tying parcels—no one below an admiral or a clergyman. There was even an identifiable Puritan gentleman who had served under Cromwell, later conformed to the established church, and emerged from all the political turmoil still owning a respectable family estate. Young women of this birth, living in a quiet country house and attending a village church scarcely bigger than a drawing room, naturally thought finery an ambition for a small trader’s daughter. There was also genteel thrift, which in those days made extravagant clothing the first expense to cut whenever money was needed for spending that better distinguished one’s rank. These reasons alone would have explained plain dress, without any religious feeling. In Miss Brooke’s case, however, religion by itself would have settled the matter. Celia gently accepted all her sister’s views, merely tempering them with the common sense that can take in momentous doctrines without any peculiar disturbance. Dorothea knew many passages of Pascal’s Pensees and Jeremy Taylor by heart. To her, human destiny viewed in the light of Christianity made the worries of women’s fashion seem an occupation for Bedlam. She could not reconcile the concerns of a spiritual life, with their eternal consequences, and a lively interest in ornamental braid and artificially puffed-out skirts. Her mind dealt in theories and naturally yearned for some exalted view of the world that could openly take in the parish of Tipton and her own conduct there. Intensity and greatness enchanted her, and she recklessly embraced anything that seemed to possess them. She was likely to seek martyrdom, to retract her beliefs, and then to suffer martyrdom after all in some unexpected place. Such traits in a marriageable girl were certainly apt to complicate her future, preventing it from being settled in the customary way by beauty, vanity and a merely doglike affection. For all this, she was not yet twenty, though the older sister. Since losing their parents at about twelve, both girls had been educated by arrangements at once restrictive and haphazard, first in an English family and then in a Swiss one at Lausanne. Their unmarried uncle and guardian had hoped in this way to make up for the disadvantages of being orphans.

Scarcely a year had passed since they came to live with their uncle at Tipton Grange. Nearly sixty, he was an agreeable man of assorted opinions and unpredictable voting habits. He had traveled when young, and in this part of the county people thought his mind had acquired too great a habit of wandering. Mr. Brooke’s conclusions were as hard to forecast as the weather. All one could safely say was that his intentions would be kindly, and that he would spend as little as possible in putting them into practice. Even the stickiest, vaguest minds contain a few hard grains of habit. A man may be careless about every interest of his own except keeping hold of his snuffbox, which he watches suspiciously and clutches with greed.

In Mr. Brooke the inherited strain of Puritan energy was plainly dormant. In his niece Dorothea it shone through virtues and faults alike, sometimes becoming impatience with her uncle’s conversation or his habit of “letting things be” on the estate. It made her long all the more to come of age and control some money for generous projects. People considered her an heiress. Besides the seven hundred pounds a year each sister had from their parents, if Dorothea married and bore a son he would inherit Mr. Brooke’s estate, thought to bring in about three thousand a year. Such a rental looked like wealth to provincial families still discussing Mr. Peel’s recent conduct on the Catholic question, unaware of the goldfields to come and of that splendid plutocracy which has so nobly raised the cost of a genteel existence.

And how could Dorothea fail to marry—a girl so beautiful, with such prospects? Only her taste for extremes could prevent it, and her determination to arrange life by ideas that might make a cautious man hesitate before proposing, or might even make her reject every proposal. A young woman of family and fortune who would suddenly kneel on a brick floor beside a sick laborer and pray fervently as though she lived in the days of the Apostles—who had strange fancies for fasting like a Papist and staying up at night over old theological books! A wife like that might wake you one fine morning with a new plan for spending her income that interfered with political economy and the keeping of riding horses. Naturally a man would think twice before risking such a partnership. Women were expected to have unsound opinions; the great protection of society and the home was that nobody acted on them. Sensible people did what their neighbors did, so that any lunatics wandering free could be recognized and avoided.

Country opinion of the new young ladies, even among the cottage dwellers, generally preferred Celia, who looked so sweet-tempered and innocent. Miss Brooke’s great eyes seemed, like her religion, too unusual and arresting. Poor Dorothea! Beside her, innocent-looking Celia was knowing and worldly: the human mind is so much subtler than the outer tissues that serve as its coat of arms or clock face.

Yet people who met Dorothea, even when this alarming gossip had prejudiced them, discovered a charm that somehow coexisted with everything they had heard. Most men found her enchanting on horseback. She loved the open air and the countryside’s changing appearances, and when combined pleasures lit up her eyes and cheeks, she looked very little like a religious devotee. Riding was an indulgence she permitted herself despite her uneasy conscience. She felt she enjoyed it with a pagan delight in the senses, and always anticipated giving it up.

She was candid, passionate and entirely without self-admiration. It was charming, indeed, to see how her imagination gave her sister Celia attractions far beyond her own. If any gentleman seemed to visit the Grange for a reason other than seeing Mr. Brooke, she concluded that he must love Celia. Sir James Chettam, for example, she always considered from Celia’s perspective, privately weighing whether accepting him would be good for her sister. The idea that anyone could regard him as her own suitor would have struck her as absurdly beside the point. Despite her eagerness to discover life’s truths, Dorothea’s ideas about marriage remained very childish. She was sure she would have accepted the judicious Hooker, had she been born in time to save him from his miserable marital mistake; or John Milton once he went blind; or any of those other great men whose odd habits it would have been gloriously devout to endure. But a pleasant, handsome baronet who answered “Exactly” even when her remarks expressed uncertainty—how could he move her as a lover? A truly delightful marriage must be one in which your husband was something like a father and could even teach you Hebrew, if you wanted.

These peculiarities in Dorothea made neighboring families blame Mr. Brooke all the more for failing to find a middle-aged lady to guide and accompany his nieces. But he so dreaded the kind of superior woman likely to be available for the post that he let Dorothea’s objections dissuade him. On this matter he was brave enough to defy the world—meaning Mrs. Cadwallader, the Rector’s wife, and the little circle of gentry with whom he exchanged visits in north-east Loamshire. So Miss Brooke ran her uncle’s household, and was by no means displeased with her new authority and the deference that went with it.

Today Sir James Chettam was to dine at the Grange with another gentleman the girls had never met, whose arrival Dorothea anticipated with a certain reverence. He was the Reverend Edward Casaubon, known throughout the county for profound learning and understood to have spent many years on a great work of religious history. He also possessed enough wealth to lend his piety luster, and opinions of his own that would become clearer when his book appeared. His very name had an impressive weight which could hardly be measured without a precise chronology of scholarship.

Earlier that day Dorothea had returned from the infant school she had established in the village. She was settling into her usual place in the pretty sitting room between the sisters’ bedrooms, intent on finishing a plan for some buildings—a kind of work she loved—when Celia, who had been watching her and hesitating over a suggestion, said—

“Dorothea, dear, if you don’t mind—if you aren’t too busy—could we look at mamma’s jewels today and divide them? It’s exactly six months today since uncle gave them to you, and you haven’t even looked at them.”

A trace of a pout shadowed Celia’s face. Her habitual awe of Dorothea and principle held the full pout back: these two connected powers could give a mysterious electric shock if carelessly touched. To her relief, Dorothea looked up with laughter in her eyes.
“What a marvellous little almanac you are, Celia! Do you mean six calendar months or six lunar ones?”

“Today is the last day of September, and uncle gave them to you on the first of April. You remember he said he’d forgotten them until then. I don’t believe you’ve thought of them since you locked them in this cabinet.”
“Well, dear, you know we’d never wear them.” Dorothea’s voice was warm and affectionate, half a caress and half an explanation. Pencil in hand, she was sketching little side plans in a margin.

Celia flushed and looked very serious. “I think, dear, we’re being disrespectful to mamma’s memory by putting them away and taking no notice of them. Besides,” she added after a little hesitation, a sob of hurt rising in her voice, “necklaces are quite usual now. Madame Poincon, who was even stricter than you about some things, used to wear ornaments. And Christians in general—surely there are women in heaven now who wore jewels.” When Celia really gave her mind to arguing, she felt she had some intellectual strength.

“You’d like to wear them?” Dorothea exclaimed. Astonished discovery animated her whole body with a theatrical movement learned from that same ornament-wearing Madame Poincon. “Well, of course, let’s get them out. Why didn’t you tell me before? But the keys, the keys!” She pressed her hands to the sides of her head, apparently despairing of her memory.
“Here they are,” said Celia, who had long thought out and prepared for this conversation.
“Please open the cabinet’s large drawer and take out the jewel box.”

Soon the open box stood before them and the jewels lay spread across the table like a bright flower bed. The collection was small, but some pieces were remarkably beautiful. The finest immediately visible were a necklace of purple amethysts in delicate gold settings, and a pearl cross set with five brilliant-cut diamonds. Dorothea picked up the necklace at once and fastened it round her sister’s neck, where it fitted nearly as tightly as a bracelet. The circle suited the Henrietta-Maria style of Celia’s head and neck, though, as she could see for herself in the tall mirror opposite.
“There, Celia! That will go with your Indian muslin. But you must wear this cross with your dark dresses.”
Celia struggled to keep from smiling with delight. “Oh, Dodo, you must keep the cross for yourself.”
“No, no, dear, no,” Dorothea answered, raising her hand in a casual gesture of refusal.
“Yes, you really must. It would look well on you—with your black dress, for instance,” Celia insisted. “Surely you _could_ wear that.”
“Not for anything, not for anything. A cross is the very last thing I’d wear as a bauble.” Dorothea gave a slight shudder.
“Then you’ll think it wicked of me to wear it,” Celia said uneasily.
“No, dear, no,” Dorothea said, stroking her sister’s cheek. “Souls have their own complexions too. What suits one won’t suit another.”
“But perhaps you’d like to keep it in memory of mamma.”
“No, I have other things of mamma’s—her sandalwood box that I love so much—plenty of things. Really, they’re all yours, dear. There’s no need to discuss it any longer. There—take your property away.”
Celia felt rather hurt. This Puritan tolerance assumed a strong superiority, scarcely easier for the fair flesh of an unenthusiastic sister to bear than Puritan persecution.
“But how can I wear jewelry when you, my older sister, won’t ever wear any?”

“Really, Celia, it’s too much to ask me to put on trinkets just to make you feel comfortable. Wearing a necklace like that would make me feel as though I’d been spinning round on my toes. The world would whirl about me, and I wouldn’t know how to walk.”

Celia had undone the necklace and taken it off. “It would be a little tight round your neck. Something that lay lower and hung down would suit you better,” she said with some satisfaction. The necklace’s complete unsuitability for Dorothea, from every point of view, made Celia happier to accept it. She was opening some ring boxes, revealing a fine emerald surrounded by diamonds, when the sun emerged from behind a cloud and cast a bright gleam across the table.

“How beautiful these stones are!” Dorothea said, swept by a new feeling as sudden as the sunlight. “It’s strange how deeply colors seem to enter us, like a scent. I suppose that’s why jewels serve as spiritual symbols in the Revelation of St. John. They look like pieces of heaven. I think that emerald is the most beautiful of all.”
“There’s a bracelet to match,” Celia said. “We didn’t notice this one at first.”

“They’re lovely,” said Dorothea, slipping the ring and bracelet onto her delicately shaped finger and wrist and raising them towards the window at eye level. All the time her mind was trying to justify her delight in their colors by blending it with her mystical religious joy.

“You _would_ like those, Dorothea,” Celia said with some hesitation, beginning to wonder at this sign of weakness in her sister. She also thought emeralds would suit her own coloring even better than purple amethysts. “You must keep the ring and bracelet, if you keep nothing else. But look, these agates are very pretty and unobtrusive.”

“Yes! I’ll keep these—the ring and bracelet,” Dorothea said. Then she lowered her hand to the table and spoke in a different tone. “Yet what wretched men must find these things, and work on them, and sell them!” She paused again. Celia thought her sister was about to give up the jewels, as consistency surely required.
“Yes, dear, I will keep these,” Dorothea said firmly. “But take everything else away, and the box as well.”
She picked up her pencil, still wearing the jewels and still looking at them. She imagined often keeping them nearby, nourishing her eyes at these little springs of pure color.
“Will you wear them when we have company?” Celia asked, watching with genuine curiosity about what her sister would do.

Dorothea shot her sister a glance. Through all the imaginative beauty with which she clothed the people she loved, a sharp perception sometimes flashed, and it could scorch. If Miss Brooke ever achieved perfect meekness, it would not be because she lacked an inward fire.
“Perhaps,” she replied rather loftily. “I can’t say how low I may sink.”

Celia blushed and felt miserable. She knew she had offended her sister, and did not dare even to say something grateful about the jewelry as she returned it to its box and carried it away. Dorothea was unhappy too. Continuing with her architectural plans, she questioned the purity of her feelings and words during the scene that had ended in that little outburst.

Celia’s own conscience assured her she had done nothing wrong. Her question had been perfectly natural and reasonable, and she kept telling herself Dorothea was inconsistent. Either she should have taken her full share of the jewels or, after saying what she had, refused them altogether.

“I’m sure—or at least I hope,” Celia thought, “that wearing a necklace won’t interfere with my prayers. And I can’t see why Dorothea’s opinions should bind me now we’re going into society, though of course they ought to bind her. But Dorothea isn’t always consistent.”
So Celia reflected, silently bending over her embroidery, until she heard her sister call.
“Here, Kitty, come and look at my plan. I’ll think myself a great architect if I haven’t put the stairs and fireplaces where they clash.”

As Celia bent over the sheet, Dorothea affectionately pressed her cheek against her sister’s arm. Celia understood. Dorothea recognized she had been wrong, and Celia forgave her. For as long as either could remember, Celia had regarded her older sister with a mixture of criticism and awe. The younger had always worn a yoke. But is there any creature under a yoke that has no private opinions?
